title: 2026 Bespoked Dresden: Curve Cycling Big Kev 32er Prototype – John Watson
content:
We’re back in Saxony at the Flughafen Dresden for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. Paul and John poked around during setup day, and John shot a pre-showcase gallery featuring the Curve Cycling Big Kev 32er prototype. Let’s check it out…

The Radavist thanks Brooks England for sponsoring our 2025 Bespoked Dresden coverage and our independent Reportage!

 

Paul and I arrived in Dresden last Wednesday night and shook off our jet lag with a pre-show shakedown on Thursday, catching up with friends and seeing what the builders and makers were rolling in during setup day. Similar to last year, I wanted to showcase a single bike to kick off our coverage, and that’s when I saw Curve’s Big Kev 32er prototype.

When Melbourne, Australia’s Curve Cycling set out to design its Big Kev 32er, the team focused on the acclaimed Big Kev 29er’s touchpoints. “We designed this size medium BK32 to have the exact same touchpoints as the medium BK29er,” Jimmy Röstlund, aka Jimmy the Swede, began to explain as I scanned the bike’s details. “With the BK32, it’s designed around a 60 mm stem (the FSA KFX Drop Stem 60 mm -20) while the 29er uses a 70 or 80 mm stem,” he continued.

This size medium prototype features a few updates to the geometry from the brand’s previous prototype debuted at the Spoken show in Australia earlier this year, which had a Mone Bikes tri-plane fork. The Big Kev 32er displayed at Bespoked was built in-house by Jimmy, who specializes in fillet brazing, and Taylor Patrick, who lays down TIG welds; the two collaborated on the tubing mitering.

Jimmy wanted to make a proper fork for the Big Kev 32er, rather than using a suspension-corrected 29er fork, which just doesn’t look right on a “ground-up” chassis design. The 29er forks also don’t use the right offset for 32ers. “We use this steel fork as a prototype for our carbon 32er fork. This allowed us to really dial in what we feel like is the perfect front-end handling,” Jimmy explained.

Jumping from a 29er diameter to 32er presented some problem-solving for the Australian brand. For starters, Jimmy had to design 3D-printed stainless dropouts that featured a 60 mm seat stay extension on them to make up for the extra wheel diameter since Curve uses pre-bent Columbus seat stays.

Curve selected Columbus Zona tubing throughout. The bottom bracket yoke and fork dropouts, which feature a 6 mm flip chip, are also 3D printed, allowing Jimmy to make offset inserts to match the flip chip that will be in the carbon fork Curve is developing for when the Big Kev 32er goes to market, which will most likely happen in the next year.

Big Kev 32er represents the skunkworks R&D division of Curve, which also rolled out a 36er back in 2021 dubbed the Titanosaur. Keeping with the dino theme, the Big Kev 32er features a paint job inspired by the Australotitan dinosaur’s 3D renders, with an earthtone ombré finish laid down in-house by Steve Varga, Curve founder and operator of the brand’s paint shop, Candy Factory Paintworks.

Be on the lookout for the production Big Kev 32er from Curve Cycling next year.
